wiki_voz_entries.title: Siguro vs. Seguro
wiki_voz_entries.description: Semantic Shift: In Spanish, 'seguro' means 'certain'. In Chavacano, influenced by Tagalog, it shifted to mean 'maybe' or 'uncertain'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Siempre
wiki_voz_entries.description: In Spanish, 'siempre' means 'always'. In Chavacano, it is used as an expression meaning 'of course' or 'naturally'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Con (Object Marker)
wiki_voz_entries.description: In Spanish, 'con' means 'with'. In Chavacano, it functions as a direct object marker (like Tagalog 'kay' or 'sa').

wiki_voz_entries.title: Masiao
wiki_voz_entries.description: Derived from Spanish 'demasiado' (too much), used locally as an intensifier similar to 'very' or 'grabe'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Rompe Cabeza
wiki_voz_entries.description: Literally 'break head'. Used locally to describe a highly difficult problem or a puzzle.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Alza Balutan
wiki_voz_entries.description: Literally 'lift the bundle'. An idiom meaning to pack up one's things and leave abruptly, often in anger.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Cara de Viernes Santo
wiki_voz_entries.description: Literally 'Good Friday face'. Used to describe someone looking extremely sad, gloomy, or depressed.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Ñor / Ñora
wiki_voz_entries.description: A localized, condensed honorific derived from Spanish 'Señor/Señora'. A deep sign of respect for elders.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Tio / Tia
wiki_voz_entries.description: Spanish for uncle/aunt, but used in Zamboanga as a polite honorific for any older stranger.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Hijo / Hija
wiki_voz_entries.description: Used affectionately by elders to address younger people, regardless of actual blood relation.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Ansina
wiki_voz_entries.description: Meaning 'like that' or 'that is how it is'. A core street-level conversational filler.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Era (Hope)
wiki_voz_entries.description: A linguistic particle added to sentences to express hope or desire, similar to Tagalog 'sana'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Manada
wiki_voz_entries.description: Derived from Spanish 'flock/herd', used in Chavacano to simply mean 'a lot' or 'many'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Vinta
wiki_voz_entries.description: A traditional outrigger boat with a colorful sail, an untranslatable cultural icon of Zamboanga.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Hermosa
wiki_voz_entries.description: Refers not just to 'beautiful', but culturally ties to the Fiesta Pilar (Zamboanga Hermosa Festival).

wiki_voz_entries.title: Camisa
wiki_voz_entries.description: Clothing term for shirt used in casual and formal contexts.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Pantalon
wiki_voz_entries.description: Clothing term for trousers or pants in common use.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Iglesia
wiki_voz_entries.description: Religious and community landmark term with strong historical continuity.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Mesa
wiki_voz_entries.description: Household table term widely used in Chavacano daily conversation.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Escuela
wiki_voz_entries.description: Education-related term used in family and institutional contexts.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Mercado
wiki_voz_entries.description: Refers to public market spaces for trade and food purchase.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Trabajo
wiki_voz_entries.description: Core livelihood term meaning work, labor, or employment.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Silla
wiki_voz_entries.description: Basic furniture term for chair inherited from Spanish usage.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Dinero
wiki_voz_entries.description: Frequent transactional term for money in commerce and household budgeting.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Fiesta
wiki_voz_entries.description: Cultural celebration term tied to local community and religious events.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Familia
wiki_voz_entries.description: Kinship term central to social identity and household life.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Ventana
wiki_voz_entries.description: Refers to a window in homes, classrooms, and offices.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Comida
wiki_voz_entries.description: General term for food and meals in domestic and public settings.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Calle
wiki_voz_entries.description: Urban navigation term for roads and streets in city discourse.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Tiempo
wiki_voz_entries.description: High-frequency term referring to time, weather, or period depending on context.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Puerta
wiki_voz_entries.description: Common word for door in household and public spaces.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Libang
wiki_voz_entries.description: In Tagalog, 'libang' means entertainment. In Cebuano, it means to defecate. A critical ML cultural patch.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Langgam
wiki_voz_entries.description: In Tagalog, it means ant. In Cebuano, it means bird. The AI must use context to translate properly.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Bitaw
wiki_voz_entries.description: In Tagalog, it means to let go. In Cebuano, it is an expression of strong agreement ('indeed' or 'really').

wiki_voz_entries.title: Sabot
wiki_voz_entries.description: In Tagalog, 'sabot' (hair). In Cebuano, it means to understand or make an agreement.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Nangita og sakit sa lawas
wiki_voz_entries.description: Literally 'looking for body aches'. Used to describe someone looking for trouble.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Gikumot ang Kasing-kasing
wiki_voz_entries.description: Literally 'heart was crumpled'. Idiom for feeling extreme emotional pain or heartbreak.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Gibaligya ang Unod
wiki_voz_entries.description: Literally 'sold the flesh'. A street-level idiom referring to sex work or extreme desperation.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Dong / Dodong
wiki_voz_entries.description: Affectionate honorific for a younger male. Patches the cold English word 'boy'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Day / Inday
wiki_voz_entries.description: Affectionate honorific for a younger female. Patches the English word 'girl' or 'miss'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Noy / Nang
wiki_voz_entries.description: Respectful honorific for an older male or female, bridging the formal gap of 'Sir/Ma'am'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Charot
wiki_voz_entries.description: Modern slang meaning 'just kidding' or 'joke only'. A crucial piece of Bislish/Street code-switching.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Chuy
wiki_voz_entries.description: Street slang for 'cool', 'handsome', or 'awesome'. Untranslatable by literal dictionary models.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Puhon
wiki_voz_entries.description: A deeply cultural expression meaning 'God willing' or 'hopefully in the future'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Habal-Habal
wiki_voz_entries.description: A highly modified motorcycle for rough terrain. Replaces the generic English 'taxi'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Pasalubong
wiki_voz_entries.description: The cultural tradition of bringing gifts from a journey. Patches the English 'souvenir'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Baga og Nawong
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: Literally 'thick face'. Used to describe someone who is shameless, audacious, or lacks basic etiquette.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Layo ra sa Tina-i
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: Literally 'far from the intestines'. A cultural idiom said to someone who gets a minor cut or injury, meaning 'it won't kill you / you will survive'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Tulog Mantika
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: Literally 'sleeping fat/oil' (like congealed cooking oil). Used to describe a very heavy sleeper who is hard to wake up.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Nag-aso ang Dunggan
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: Literally 'ears are smoking'. Translates the English intent of someone being furiously angry.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Namuti ang Mata
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: Literally 'eyes turned white'. Used when someone has been waiting for a very long time.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Lawom og Bulsa
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: Literally 'deep pockets'. While in English it means rich, in Cebuano it means someone who is extremely stingy or cheap.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Kuskos Balungos
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: Describes unnecessary delays, too many trivial complaints, or overly complicated procedures.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Basa ang Papel
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: Literally 'wet paper'. Means someone has a ruined reputation or is no longer trusted in the community.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Walay Kukaluoy
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: Absolutely ruthless, without a single drop of pity or mercy.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Gipahilak og Lansang
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: Literally 'made to cry nails'. Meaning someone was put through extreme hardship or severe suffering.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Gasa sa Kahitas-an
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: 'Gift from above'. A deeply cultural and spiritual idiom representing a blessing or miracle.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Hugas Kamot
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: Literally 'washing hands'. Meaning to deny any involvement or escape responsibility from a problem.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Bai / Bay
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: A ubiquitous term for 'friend' or 'buddy'. The ultimate peer-to-peer honorific among Cebuano males.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Migo
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Derived from Spanish 'amigo', a casual yet polite way to address a male peer or acquaintance.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Miga
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: A casual yet polite way to address a female peer, waitress, or acquaintance.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Tay / Tatay
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: 'Father', but broadly used as a high-respect honorific for any elderly man, transcending family lines.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Nay / Nanay
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: 'Mother', but broadly used to address any elderly woman with deep communal respect.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Iyo / Tiyo
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Uncle. Used locally to address middle-aged men politely.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Iya / Tiya
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Aunt. Used locally to address middle-aged women politely.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Maninoy
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Godfather. Carries immense sociolinguistic weight in the Visayas due to the Compadrazgo system.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Maninay
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Godmother. A deeply respected honorific bridging religious and social family structures.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Kol / Ankol
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Localized spelling of 'Uncle'. Street-level honorific used heavily for drivers, guards, or older strangers.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Ante / Anti
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Localized spelling of 'Auntie'. Street-level honorific for female vendors or strangers.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Bos / Boss
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: English loanword entirely co-opted by Visayan street culture as a polite greeting for male strangers.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Libog
wiki_voz_entries.description: Critical False Cognate: In Tagalog, 'libog' means sexual lust. In Cebuano, it simply means 'confused' or 'confusing'. Prevents massive AI context failures.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Hilo
wiki_voz_entries.description: False Cognate: In Tagalog, 'hilo' means dizzy. In Cebuano, it means 'poison'. A mistranslation here can alter severe medical context.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Hubad
wiki_voz_entries.description: False Cognate: In Tagalog, 'hubad' means naked. In Cebuano, it is the exact verb for 'to translate' or 'to untie'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Palit
wiki_voz_entries.description: False Cognate: In Tagalog, 'palit' means to exchange or swap. In Cebuano, it means 'to buy'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Lagot
wiki_voz_entries.description: False Cognate: In Tagalog, it means 'you are in trouble' (Lagot ka!). In Cebuano, it means 'angry' or 'annoyed' (Nalagot ko).

wiki_voz_entries.title: Usa
wiki_voz_entries.description: False Cognate: In Tagalog, 'usa' is a deer. In Cebuano, it is the number 'one'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Giatay
wiki_voz_entries.description: Expression: A highly common expletive or expression of intense frustration/surprise. Literally translates to a chicken liver disease.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Simbako
wiki_voz_entries.description: Expression: 'God forbid' or 'Knock on wood'. Used to ward off bad luck when someone says something negative.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Kuan
wiki_voz_entries.description: Expression: The ultimate Cebuano placeholder word. Used when the speaker forgets a noun, verb, or adjective, similar to 'whatchamacallit'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Hasola
wiki_voz_entries.description: Expression: Derived from the English 'hassle'. Used constantly to describe a deeply inconvenient or annoying situation.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Pag Sure Oy
wiki_voz_entries.description: Expression: Bislish street phrase meaning 'Are you kidding me?', 'Be serious', or 'Come on!'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Bakal
wiki_voz_entries.description: In Tagalog, it means 'iron' or 'metal'. In Hiligaynon, it means 'to buy'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Sira
wiki_voz_entries.description: In Tagalog, 'sira' means broken. In Hiligaynon, it means 'to close' (the door/window).

wiki_voz_entries.title: Pata
wiki_voz_entries.description: In Tagalog, 'pata' is pork hock/leg. In Hiligaynon, 'pata' means feeling extremely tired or exhausted.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Tulog vs. Tolog
wiki_voz_entries.description: Similar to Tagalog, but in Ilonggo syntax, context determines if it means 'asleep' or 'sleeping late'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Gindakop sang kamingaw
wiki_voz_entries.description: Literally 'caught by loneliness'. Deep Ilonggo idiom for severe homesickness.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Nagapanago ang adlaw
wiki_voz_entries.description: Literally 'the sun is hiding'. Used to describe overcast, gloomy weather.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Gintuka sang manok
wiki_voz_entries.description: Literally 'pecked by a chicken'. Used to describe someone who acts crazy or irrational.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Toto
wiki_voz_entries.description: Affectionate honorific for a younger male. A cultural cornerstone of Panay politeness.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Inday
wiki_voz_entries.description: Affectionate honorific for a younger female, showing endearment beyond the English 'girl'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Palangga
wiki_voz_entries.description: A term of deep endearment used for loved ones, mapping to 'darling' or 'beloved'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Baw / Ay Abaw
wiki_voz_entries.description: An expression of surprise, amazement, or sometimes dismay. Similar to 'Wow' or 'Oh my'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Te
wiki_voz_entries.description: A conversational filler meaning 'So', 'Therefore', or 'Well...'. Highly contextual.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Tikalon
wiki_voz_entries.description: Street slang for someone who is extremely boastful or arrogant.

wiki_voz_entries.title: La Paz Batchoy
wiki_voz_entries.description: Untranslatable culinary culture. A famous noodle soup from Iloilo.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Kansi
wiki_voz_entries.description: An Ilonggo sour soup. Replaces generic English terms like 'stew' with strict cultural accuracy.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Wala Untat nga Baba
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: 'Non-stop mouth'. Used to describe an incessant gossiper or someone who talks too much.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Gapangita bato ipukpok sa ulo
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: 'Looking for a stone to hit one's head'. Creating unnecessary problems for oneself.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Naga-init ang Ulo
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: 'Head is heating up'. The universal Visayan idiom for losing one's temper.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Galupad ang Utok
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: 'Flying brain'. Used to describe someone daydreaming or not paying attention.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Balhas sang Imol
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: 'Sweat of the poor'. Represents extremely hard, exhausting physical labor.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Basa nga Idik
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: 'Wet piglet'. Used to describe someone who is completely drenched in sweat or rain.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Malapad ang Papel
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: 'Wide paper'. Means someone has strong influence or connections in high places.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Gindakop sang Katulog
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: 'Caught by sleep'. Accidentally falling asleep due to extreme exhaustion.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Hugas Kamot
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: 'Washing hands'. Refusing to take accountability for a mistake.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Buhi ang Dugo
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: 'Blood is alive'. Feeling suddenly energized or excited.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Kigol sang Baso
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: 'Bottom of the glass'. Describes incredibly thick eyeglasses.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Nagapangita sang Gamo
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: Actively looking for a fight or looking to start an argument.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Nonoy / Noy
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Affectionate term for a young boy, often carried into adulthood by family.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Nene / Neneng
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Affectionate term for a young girl in the community.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Manong / Nong
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Respectful address for an older male, bridging the English gap of 'Sir/Mister'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Manang / Nang
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Respectful address for an older female.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Tay / Tatay
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Broad honorific for any elderly man.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Nay / Nanay
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Broad honorific for any elderly woman.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Tiyo / Tiya
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Uncle/Aunt, used formally for middle-aged community members.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Pare / Kumpare
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Close male friend or co-sponsor in religious rites.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Mare / Kumare
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Close female friend or co-sponsor.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Mig / Migo
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Friendly, casual term for a male acquaintance.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Miga
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Friendly, casual term for a female acquaintance.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Boss
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: English loanword adopted natively as a respectful street-greeting.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Sabot
wiki_voz_entries.description: False Cognate: In Cebuano, 'sabot' means to understand. In Hiligaynon, it refers to pubic hair. Critical ML patch.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Pating
wiki_voz_entries.description: False Cognate: In Tagalog, it means shark. In Hiligaynon, it is a pigeon/dove.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Libang
wiki_voz_entries.description: False Cognate: Like Cebuano, means 'defecate', completely contradicting Tagalog 'entertainment'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Basa
wiki_voz_entries.description: False Cognate Context: Can mean 'wet' or 'read' depending strictly on sentence structure.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Sugid
wiki_voz_entries.description: False Cognate: In some Visayan dialects it implies a story, in Hiligaynon it strictly means 'to confess' or 'tattle'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Utong
wiki_voz_entries.description: False Cognate: In Tagalog, it refers to a body part. In Hiligaynon, it means to hold one's breath.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Ahay
wiki_voz_entries.description: Expression: Untranslatable sigh denoting sympathy, pity, or sadness.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Ambot
wiki_voz_entries.description: Expression: 'I don't know'. Culturally heavier than the English equivalent, often showing mild annoyance.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Gali
wiki_voz_entries.description: Expression: A particle expressing sudden realization, similar to 'Oh, I see!'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Haw
wiki_voz_entries.description: Expression: Interrogative particle attached to the end of sentences for emphasis ('Why is that so?').

wiki_voz_entries.title: Mu / Amo
wiki_voz_entries.description: Expression: Assent filler meaning 'Yes, exactly' or 'That is correct'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Embarazada
wiki_voz_entries.description: False Cognate: Sounds like 'embarrassed' in English, but actually means 'pregnant'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Constipado
wiki_voz_entries.description: False Cognate: Sounds like 'constipated' in English, but actually means having a cold or being congested.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Asistir
wiki_voz_entries.description: False Cognate: Sounds like 'assist', but actually means 'to attend' (a meeting or event).

wiki_voz_entries.title: Éxito
wiki_voz_entries.description: False Cognate: Sounds like 'exit', but actually means 'success'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Tomar el Pelo
wiki_voz_entries.description: Literally 'to take the hair'. An idiom that means to tease someone or pull their leg.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Estar en las nubes
wiki_voz_entries.description: Literally 'to be in the clouds'. Means to be daydreaming or distracted.

trigger_words: tirar la casa por la ventana
wiki_voz_entries.title: Tirar la casa por la ventana
wiki_voz_entries.description: Literally 'throw the house through the window'. Means to spare no expense or throw a massive party.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Don / Doña
wiki_voz_entries.description: A formal prefix of respect used before a person's first name, bridging a deep cultural politeness gap.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Usted
wiki_voz_entries.description: The formal 'You'. Essential for sociolinguistic politeness when addressing authority.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Caballero
wiki_voz_entries.description: Used formally to address a gentleman, carrying more chivalrous weight than the English 'Sir'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Vale
wiki_voz_entries.description: Slang/Filler used heavily in Spain meaning 'okay', 'alright', or 'sounds good'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Hombre
wiki_voz_entries.description: Literally 'man', but used as an interjection to show surprise, agreement, or emphasis ('Oh man!').

wiki_voz_entries.title: Guay
wiki_voz_entries.description: Colloquial slang meaning 'cool' or 'awesome'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Siesta
wiki_voz_entries.description: A cultural midday nap or rest period. A localized concept globally recognized.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Tapas
wiki_voz_entries.description: Small cultural appetizers or snacks served with drinks. Replaces generic English 'food'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Dar a luz
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: Literally 'give to light'. Translates strictly to giving birth.

trigger_words: costar un ojo de la cara
wiki_voz_entries.title: Costar un ojo de la cara
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: 'Cost an eye from the face'. Means something is incredibly expensive.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Pan comido
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: 'Eaten bread'. Maps to the English 'piece of cake' or very easy.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Meter la pata
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: 'Put the leg in'. Means to make a huge mistake or say the wrong thing.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Hacer la vista gorda
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: 'Make the fat view'. Means to intentionally turn a blind eye to a rule being broken.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Ponerse las pilas
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: 'Put in your batteries'. Means to wake up, focus, and get to work.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Ser la oveja negra
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: 'To be the black sheep'. Cross-cultural idiom for the outcast of a family.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Hablar por los codos
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: 'Talk through the elbows'. Describes a person who talks excessively.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Irse por las ramas
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: 'Go through the branches'. Means to digress or beat around the bush.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Quedarse de piedra
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: 'To stay of stone'. To be utterly shocked or stunned into silence.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Llamar al pan, pan
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: 'Call bread bread'. To speak bluntly and tell the truth (call a spade a spade).

wiki_voz_entries.title: Estar hasta las narices
wiki_voz_entries.description: Idiomatic Patch: 'To be up to the noses'. Means to be completely fed up or sick of something.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Señor
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Standard formal address for an older or authoritative male.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Señora
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Standard formal address for an older or married female.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Señorita
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Formal and polite address for an unmarried younger woman.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Jefe
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Boss. Used socially to show respect to a manager or leader.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Patrón
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Heavy sociolinguistic title for a land-owner or senior boss.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Maestro
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Teacher or master, heavily used in trade to respect expertise.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Padre
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Father, but heavily embedded as a religious/respectful title.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Madre
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Mother, carrying deep cultural and religious reverence.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Tío
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Uncle, but in Spain it serves as the universal slang for 'guy' or 'dude'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Tía
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Aunt, but heavily used as slang for 'girl' or 'woman'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Colega
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Colleague or friend, showing peer-to-peer respect.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Su Majestad
wiki_voz_entries.description: Politeness Gap: Your Majesty. A legacy honorific required by the NLLB base models for historical texts.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Actualmente
wiki_voz_entries.description: False Cognate: Looks like 'actually', but means 'currently' or 'nowadays'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Carpeta
wiki_voz_entries.description: False Cognate: Looks like 'carpet', but means a 'folder' or 'file'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Fábrica
wiki_voz_entries.description: False Cognate: Looks like 'fabric', but means a 'factory'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Recordar
wiki_voz_entries.description: False Cognate: Looks like 'record' (audio/video), but means 'to remember'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Sopa
wiki_voz_entries.description: False Cognate: Looks like 'soap', but is actually 'soup'. AI must catch this to prevent bizarre translations.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Largo
wiki_voz_entries.description: False Cognate: Looks like 'large', but actually means 'long' in length.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Venga
wiki_voz_entries.description: Expression: Filler word meaning 'come on', 'alright', or 'hurry up'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Madre mía
wiki_voz_entries.description: Expression: 'My mother'. Intense expression of surprise or shock, like 'Oh my God!'.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Chaval
wiki_voz_entries.description: Expression: Common slang for a kid, youth, or young person.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Fiesta
wiki_voz_entries.description: Expression/Culture: The untranslatable cultural weight of a Spanish party or celebration.

wiki_voz_entries.title: Olé
wiki_voz_entries.description: Expression: Classic exclamation of approval or encouragement.
